reading.rtitle: The Week That Will Not Shrink
paras: Every few years a report appears which claims that the five-day week is finished. The trials that get the headlines are the ones in which output held steady while hours fell, and they are real: firms in Iceland, Britain and Japan have all published numbers that bear out the basic claim. What the headlines leave out is the caveat, which is that almost every trial measured the same narrow thing. Output, in an office, is usually a proxy for something nobody can count directly, and the trials that reported the biggest gains were mostly run in firms whose work was already easy to measure.

A case in point is software. A team whose week is organized around discrete tasks can lose a day and make it up by cutting meetings, which is exactly what most trials found. A hospital cannot. Nor can a court, a restaurant or a factory, where the output is the hour itself. This is where the sweeping version of the argument, the one that says the four-day week works, starts to come apart: the idea has gained traction fastest in the industries that needed it least, and has lagged behind badly everywhere the work is tied to a person being physically present.

None of this means the shorter week is a fantasy, and it would be easy to overstate the objection. The honest position is that the whole case hinges on measurement, and that our habit of counting hours is entrenched for a reason: hours are the one thing everybody can agree on. The downside of a proxy is that it eventually gets managed instead of the thing it stands for. Any serious version of this reform, therefore, is at odds with the way most organizations currently decide who is working hard, which is a much harder problem than the calendar.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: The four-day week has been proved to work in every industry, and only tradition is stopping it.
The evidence for the four-day week is real but narrow: it comes from the industries that are easiest to measure, and the real problem is how we count work at all.
Shorter working weeks reduce output everywhere, which is why the trials were abandoned.

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: The trials that get the headlines are the ones that measured the easiest thing.
A team whose week is built around discrete tasks can absorb the change.
This is the point at which the sweeping version starts to come apart.
The whole case hinges on how you measure output.
Iceland, which ran the largest trial, published the numbers in full.
The habit that is hardest to change is the one nobody has to defend.

listenings.text: The thing I keep having to explain about the four-day week evidence is that it is real and it is narrow at the same time, and people hear only one of those. Yes, the trials found what they say they found. But look at who volunteered. A firm that puts its hand up for a study like this is already a firm that thinks it has slack in the week, and that is not a random sample of the economy. My own view, for what it is worth, is that the interesting number is not output at all. It is turnover. In almost every trial I have read, the people stayed, and staff who stay are cheaper than staff you have to replace twice a year. If somebody made the argument on those grounds I would find it much harder to argue with, and nobody does, because turnover is slow and headlines are not.

We ran it for six months and I would do it again, with two conditions that nobody warned me about. The first is that you have to kill meetings before you cut the day, not after. We tried it the other way round for three weeks and simply compressed the same chaos into less time, and everybody was miserable. The second is that it does not land evenly. The teams whose work is project-based barely noticed. Our support desk, which has to answer a phone that rings whether or not it is Friday, absorbed the whole cost of it, and I did not see that coming until the complaints started arriving from inside the building. So my honest summary is that it worked, that the reporting on it is far too tidy, and that anybody who tells you it is simply a scheduling decision has never run one.
